sm: Michael Foster opens a talk titled The Holy War in Antioch, how to fight with brothers, by reading Acts 15, verses 36 to 41, where Paul and Barnabas split over taking John Mark along. He jokes about Norm Macdonald being fired from Saturday Night Live and later returning, using it to explain his own return to a Confederation of Reformed Evangelical Churches event after leaving that denomination over a disagreement about paedocommunion. He says he still disagrees on that point but shares the essentials of the faith with them. He then gives six principles from Acts 15, starting with the first: conflict is a normal and necessary part of the Christian life, and Christians must learn to handle it in a godly way.

Foster distinguishes peace from mere quiet, saying real peace means wholeness and that the doorway to peace is often conflict, as in a church that feels different after a contentious person is removed. His second principle is that some conflicts are too sharp and complicated to resolve quickly and need outside help. He says everyday admonishing between believers, which is the first step of church discipline, keeps small problems from becoming explosions, and he cites the Jerusalem council as a case for church government and connectionalism. He lists rules for fighting: Matthew 18 for personal offenses, Titus 3 for divisive men, and Proverbs 19 for offenses that should simply be overlooked and not kept in your pocket for later.

Foster describes a sharp fight with a pastor friend that was kept within the elders and never dragged the church into it. He criticizes social media blowups and says to sit on posts overnight before deciding whether something should be private or public. He says to act in ways that honor God regardless of outcome. His third principle is that intense conflicts are often fueled by family, friendship, political and financial factors. He notes Mark was a relative of Barnabas, and he cites Matthew Henry and Calvin on guarding against partiality. He also points to Barnabas being swept along by hypocrisy in Galatians 2.

Foster says social pressure changes behavior even when the theology stays the same, and that an elder whose relative is under discipline may need to recuse himself. He warns that loyalties, fear and reputation can sway judgment, though not every disagreement reduces to psychology. He criticizes people hopping between popular teachers, saying he wants to be a brother and a pastor, not a hero, and that fanboys turn into haters. His fourth principle is that many conflicts come from good things that are wrongly ordered. Paul and Barnabas both wanted the gospel to advance, but disagreed on whether restoring Mark meant putting him straight back into that role. He cites Peter's rebuke in Matthew 16 and Jesus on loving family in Matthew 10.

Foster says Jesus is ordering our loves, not condemning them, and that forgiveness does not automatically mean restoration to every responsibility. Paul later called Mark useful for ministry, so saying no to Mark was a way of being for him. He argues the church needs more nos, and tells of being told no at a church planting assessment, and of confronting a drunk friend on a porch out of love. His fifth principle is that many conflicts end in messy resolutions, with the Jerusalem Council settling the gospel question while asking for practical accommodations for fellowship. He says Paul was probably right about Mark, though Calvin allows both men may have gone too far in the heat of the dispute.

Foster says you can be right about a decision and still have something to repent of in how you handled it. He talks about arguing with his wife Emily early in their marriage, and says sometimes it is enough to apologize, forgive, and go to bed. He says he did not answer every accusation after leaving the denomination, because sometimes you must live with being misunderstood and leave hidden things to God, citing First Corinthians 4:5. He has reconciled somewhat with the pastor he fought, and says never take a pound of flesh when an ounce will do. His sixth principle is that not every conflict deserves your attention. Quoting Proverbs 26:17, he says meddling in other people's quarrels is like grabbing a dog by the ears.

Foster notes that Paul's first impulse was to check on the churches he was responsible for, and he urges listeners to start with their own marriage, children and church. He says online disputes feel close and let people feel courageous while avoiding hard conversations at home, and he cites First Thessalonians 4:11 about living quietly. In conclusion, he says he planned something more controversial but felt many listeners were tired from conflict and lost partnerships, and that the intense pressure of the earlier pandemic and political era has faded into a grind of getting to know each other. He exhorts them to pursue peace wherever possible but stand firm where they must, putting truth and Christ's cause first, and closes with a prayer.
